question: What is the primary construction of the DA 40 D's fuselage?

options.text: A GFRP semi monocoque molded construction
A riveted aluminum semi monocoque construction
A welded steel tube truss with fabric covering
A carbon-fiber-only monocoque with no GFRP

explanation: The fuselage is of semi monocoque molded GFRP construction, with the firewall's fire protection covered on the engine side by stainless steel cladding.

question: How are the DA 40 D's wings constructed, and what fail-safe concept do they use?

options.text: Aluminum sandwich panels bonded to a GFRP spar
GFRP/CFRP sandwich construction, each wing with a top and bottom shell
Aluminum spar and rib construction with a fabric skin
A single GFRP shell with no separate top and bottom halves

explanation: Each wing has a front and rear spar plus a top shell and a bottom shell - a 'fail-safe' concept - built principally of GFRP/CFRP sandwich construction, the same material used for the ailerons and flaps.

question: What tail configuration does the DA 40 D have, and what is it made from?

options.text: A cruciform tail of GFRP sandwich construction throughout
A 'T' tail of aluminum semi monocoque construction
A 'T' tail of GFRP semi monocoque construction
A conventional low-set tail of aluminum construction

explanation: The airplane has a 'T' tail of GFRP semi monocoque construction; both stabilizers have twin spars and a skin with no sandwich, while the rudder and elevator are sandwich construction.

question: What is the flap position indicator light meaning, and where is it in the flight-controls-adjacent instrument panel layout?

options.text: Green upper light = LDG; white center = T/O; white lower = Cruise (UP)
White upper light = Cruise (UP); green center = T/O; green lower = LDG
Green upper light = T/O; white center = Cruise (UP); white lower = LDG
Green upper light = Cruise (UP); white center = T/O; white lower = LDG

explanation: Three lights beside the flap selector switch show flap position: green (upper) for Cruise/UP, white (center) for T/O, white (lower) for LDG; two lit together means the flaps are in transit.

question: What are the two example instrument panel variants described in the AFM?

options.text: VFR and IFR
Analog and Glass (G1000)
Standard and Long Range
Day and Night

explanation: Because the DA 40 D can be equipped with numerous instrument panel variants, the AFM describes only two examples: VFR and IFR.

question: Besides the movable nozzles in the instrument panel, where else are cockpit ventilation nozzles found?

options.text: In the wing roots, ducted through the flap torque tube
Spherical nozzles in the roll bar beside the front seats and on the central console above the passengers' heads
Only in the rear door, for the rear passengers
Only under the front seats

explanation: In addition to the instrument panel nozzles, spherical nozzles in the roll bar (left and right, next to the front seats) and on the central console provide ventilation; they are opened and closed by twisting.

question: What type of landing gear is fitted to the DA 40 D?

options.text: A retractable tricycle gear with hydraulically actuated main struts
A fixed tricycle gear with oleo-pneumatic main struts
A fixed tricycle gear with sprung steel main struts and a free-castering nose wheel
A fixed tailwheel gear with sprung steel main struts

explanation: The landing gear is fixed tricycle: sprung steel struts on the main gear, and a free-castering nose wheel sprung by an elastomer package.

question: What springs the nose wheel, in contrast to the main gear's sprung steel struts?

options.text: An oleo-pneumatic shock strut
A leaf-spring assembly
The same sprung steel construction as the main gear
An elastomer package

explanation: The free-castering nose wheel is sprung by an elastomer package rather than a steel strut.

question: What is noted about flying the DA 40 D with the wheel fairings removed?

options.text: There is a reduction in some areas of performance
There is no measurable performance effect
It is prohibited outright under all circumstances
It improves climb performance by reducing drag asymmetry

explanation: The wheel fairings are removable, but the AFM notes a reduction in some areas of performance when flying without them.

question: What type of wheel brakes does the DA 40 D use, and how are they actuated?

options.text: Pneumatic disk brakes, actuated by toe pedals
Hydraulically operating disk brakes, individually actuated by toe pedals
Mechanically operated drum brakes, actuated by a hand lever
Hydraulically operating disk brakes, actuated only by the parking brake lever

explanation: Hydraulically operating disk brakes act on the main gear wheels, individually operated by toe pedals.

question: Where is the parking brake lever located, and in what position are the brakes released?

options.text: Beside the power lever on the large center console; upper position is released
On the left sidewall next to the fuel valve; upper position is released
On the small center console under the instrument panel; upper position is released
On the small center console under the instrument panel; lower position is released

explanation: The parking brake lever sits on the small center console under the instrument panel, in the upper position when released; pulling it down until it catches sets the brake.

question: What material combination is used for the seats to increase passive safety?

options.text: Solid aluminum frames with foam cushions only
GFRP only, with no energy-absorbing elements
Steel tube frames with leather upholstery
A carbon fiber/Kevlar hybrid material and GFRP, with energy-absorbing foam elements

explanation: The seats use a carbon fiber/Kevlar hybrid material and GFRP for passive safety, with removable furnishings and energy-absorbing foam elements.

question: What is required before any baggage may be loaded into the baggage compartment?

options.text: A baggage net must be fitted - without it, no baggage may be loaded
The rear seats must be removed entirely
The Long Range Tank must not be installed
The baggage must weigh less than 10 kg regardless of the net

explanation: Without a baggage net fitted, no baggage may be loaded into the compartment behind the rear seat backs.

question: Under what condition may the front canopy be flown in the 'cooling gap' position?

options.text: In flight, but only below 120 KIAS
On the ground only - it must be completely closed and locked before take-off
At any time in flight below 10000 ft
Only during taxi with the engine at idle

explanation: The 'cooling gap' position, which leaves a gap under the canopy, is for ground use only; before take-off the canopy must be completely closed and locked.

question: Why should the front canopy not be blocked with its locking key before flight?

options.text: Because it would trigger the DOOR warning light continuously
Because it interferes with the cooling gap function
To assure emergency evacuation from outside is still possible
Because the key mechanism is not rated for flight loads

explanation: Locking the canopy with the key before flight is specifically warned against, since it would prevent emergency evacuation from outside.

question: What prevents the rear door from dropping once opened, and what protects it against unintentional opening in flight?

options.text: A simple friction hinge prevents it dropping; a spring latch guards against opening
An electric actuator holds it open; a solenoid lock guards against opening
A counterweight prevents it dropping; a second door handle guards against opening
A gas pressure damper prevents it dropping; an additional lever guards against unintentional opening

explanation: A gas pressure damper holds the rear door open (though it must be held in strong winds), and it is protected against unintentional opening in flight by an additional lever.

question: On the heating and ventilation controls, what does moving the central air distribution lever up select?

options.text: Airflow to the canopy (DEFROST)
Airflow to the floor (FLOOR)
Heating OFF
Heating ON

explanation: The central (air distribution) lever selects DEFROST (airflow to canopy) when up and FLOOR (airflow to floor) when down; the separate left lever controls heating ON/OFF.

question: If installed under OÄM 40-326, where is the emergency axe stowed?

options.text: Clipped to the instrument panel
On the floor panel under the co-pilot's seat
In the baggage compartment
Behind the pilot seat, next to the fuel quantity measuring device

explanation: The optional emergency axe, used to break through the canopy if it cannot be opened, is stowed on the floor panel under the co-pilot's seat.

question: Where is total pressure measured for the Pitot-static system?

options.text: At two orifices on the vertical stabilizer
At the nose of the fuselage, ahead of the propeller
At the leading edge of a Pitot probe under the left wing
At the leading edge of a Pitot probe under the right wing

explanation: Total pressure is measured at the leading edge of the Pitot probe under the left wing; static pressure comes from two orifices at the lower and rear edges of the same probe.

question: If the Pitot-static system fails, what alternative static pressure source can the pilot select?

options.text: A second Pitot probe under the right wing
Ambient pressure sensed by the ECU's manifold pressure sensor
There is no alternative source available
Cabin static pressure, via the alternate static valve

explanation: The alternate static valve lets cabin static pressure be used as the static source if the Pitot-static system fails.

question: How does the stall warning system alert the pilot, and what activates it?

options.text: A horn sounds, activated by suction at an orifice on the left wing leading edge
A red light illuminates, activated by an angle-of-attack vane on the right wing
A stick shaker is driven electrically from the AED
An aural tone is generated by the ECU based on airspeed alone

explanation: Suction at an orifice on the left wing's leading edge - marked by a red ring - activates the stall warning horn in the instrument panel via a hose, growing louder closer to the stall.

question: Approximately how far above stalling speed does the stall warning horn begin to sound?

options.text: Approximately 15 to a minimum of 10 knots above stalling speed
Approximately 10 to a minimum of 5 knots above stalling speed
Approximately 20 to a minimum of 15 knots above stalling speed
Exactly 5 knots above stalling speed, with no range given

explanation: The stall warning horn sounds when airspeed drops to approximately 10 down to a minimum of 5 knots above the stalling speed.

question: How many headset connection points are provided between the front seats?

options.text: Up to 3
Only 1, for the pilot
Up to 4
Up to 2

explanation: Connection facilities for up to 4 headsets are provided between the front seats, alongside a push-to-talk button on each control stick.
